source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC7146100 (JAMA Network Open, published version, not an author manuscript), read in full in my own browser tab on 2026-10-27 and saved to my scratch folder; Tables 1 to 3 from the HTML text; Figure 2 (forest plot) read as an image and zoomed; Figure 1 (PRISMA flowchart) not viewed; online supplement not read. Card check (step 2) done on 2026-10-30 from the saved text (the browser could not be reached that day); the article notes (author contributions, conflict-of-interest disclosures, additional contributions) were read in the page on 2026-10-31.

claims.overstatement: None as far as Bahji et al. are concerned: the claim is more cautious than the review, which presents 47% as the prevalence among people with regular or dependent use and says in its Conclusions that withdrawal was more common in men. 'Depended strongly on where the sample came from' describes between-study differences in pooled prevalence, which is how the source reports them; it is not an effect of setting, and the claim does not say it is.
claims.note: Every Bahji number in the statement and magnitude re-found. (1) The population interval 13 to 22 is Table 2's; the abstract and the Results 5th paragraph print 13% to 21%, and Figure 2 prints 0.16 (0.13 to 0.20). (2) The overall 47% (41% to 52%) is the abstract's; the Results 4th paragraph prints 27% to 37%, and Figure 2 prints random effects 0.46 (0.37 to 0.55) and fixed effect 0.28 (0.27 to 0.28). (3) Inpatient n 357 is the text's; Table 1 and Figure 2 give 359. (4) Editors' calculations recomputed: 6,469 of 23,518 = 27.5% (I get 27.51%); Figure 2's event column sums to exactly 6,469, so this is the review's own participant-level count; Table 1 cohort size x prevalence sums to 6,470.0, which is the magnitude's 6,470 (the statement's 6,469 is the abstract's figure; harmonize, both give 27.5%). Unweighted mean of the 50 cohort prevalences in Table 1 = 47.5% (median 49.1%), so 'close to the plain average' holds; the 35 clinical cohorts hold 6,043 of 23,518 participants (25.7%). (5) Only one population cohort used DSM-5 (Livne et al. 2019: 1,527, 12.1%; Figure 2: 185 of 1,527). (6) Bahji's own DSM-5 summary lists 'sleep disturbance' and 'appetite or weight disturbance'; the claim's 'less appetite or weight loss' is the DSM-5 wording, presumably from Connor et al. (2021). The abstract's Importance section places withdrawal on cessation of heavy and prolonged use, a DSM-5 condition the claim's definition leaves out (it says only stopping or cutting down); consider adding it. (7) 'Most predate DSM-5': 46 of the 50 cohorts in Table 1 used DSM-III-R or DSM-IV criteria. (8) The lifetime against past-year contrast, like the tobacco meta-regression, compares studies, not people, and is entangled with setting.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Data Sources; Abstract › Study Selection; Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Eight databases searched from inception to 19 June 2019, plus reference lists and PubMed similar articles; inclusion: English-language observational studies whose primary group had regular use of cannabinoids or cannabis use disorder, reporting withdrawal prevalence measured with a validated instrument; the definition of regular use varied between cohorts; case reports, series and abstracts excluded.

47 articles reporting 50 cohorts with 23,518 participants: 15 population-based (30%), 28 outpatient (56%), 7 inpatient (14%); 18 cohorts reported lifetime and 32 past-year withdrawal; overall pooled prevalence 47% (95% CI 41% to 52%), 6,469 of 23,518, I2 99.2%.

Overall pooled prevalence 47% printed with a 95% CI of 27% to 37%, which excludes the estimate; I2 99.2%, 50 studies, 23,518 participants; cohort estimates ranged from 8% to 100%; setting estimates given here as 0.16 (0.13 to 0.20), 0.54 (0.49 to 0.59) and 0.87 (0.77 to 0.93), with the outpatient value labelled inpatient.

Population-based 17% (Table 2: 13 to 22; text: 13% to 21%), 15 cohorts, 17,475 participants, I2 98%; outpatient 54% (48 to 59), 28 cohorts, 5,684 participants, I2 92% in the text and 94% in Table 2; inpatient 87% (79 to 94), 7 cohorts, 357 participants, I2 74% in the text and 94% in Table 2; difference between settings P < .001 (chi-square printed as 0.172).

anchors.locator: Table 2 (Timeline of CWS; Study design); Results, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Past-year withdrawal 31% (27 to 36), 32 cohorts, I2 99%; lifetime 76% (70 to 82), 18 cohorts, I2 86%; lifetime estimates significantly higher (P < .001). Cross-sectional studies 19% (15 to 24; 17 cohorts) against cohort studies 62% (56 to 68; 33).

anchors.locator: Table 1 (Livne et al. 2019 row); Figure 2 (Setting: population)
anchors.extracted: The only population cohort with DSM-5 criteria for both use disorder and withdrawal: 1,527 participants, 24.6% with cannabis use disorder, withdrawal 12.1% (Figure 2: 185 of 1,527, 0.12, 0.11 to 0.14). Table 1 lists 4 DSM-5 cohorts in all (the other 3 outpatient); Table 2 counts 5.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (Sex); Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Conclusions
anchors.extracted: Men 27% (21 to 34) and women 26% (19 to 33), 15 studies each, P = .99; the Discussion says withdrawal was not associated with sex, while the Conclusions say it was more common in men.

DSM-5 withdrawal as the review summarises it: at least 3 of 7 symptoms developing within 7 days of reduced use (irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep disturbance; appetite or weight disturbance; restlessness; depressed mood; somatic symptoms such as headache, sweating, nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain). The abstract's Importance section says withdrawal occurs on cessation of heavy and prolonged use.
The definition of regular use varied across cohorts and is not given for each cohort; where a study used several cut points, the lowest threshold for withdrawal was taken.

Univariable study-level meta-regressions: share with tobacco use beta 0.002 (26 studies, P = .02); share using daily beta 0.004 (48, P < .001); share with cannabis use disorder beta 0.005 (48, P < .001); other drug use beta 0.003 (11, P = .05); share with alcohol use (17, P = .97), psychiatric disorder (16, P = .93) and mean age (48, P = .10) not associated.

Cohort size x withdrawal prevalence sums to 6,470.0 of 23,518 (27.5%); the unweighted mean of the 50 cohort prevalences is 47.5% (median 49.1%; range 7.6% to 100%); crude proportions 18.6% (population), 51.5% (outpatient), 82.2% (inpatient); the 35 clinical cohorts hold 6,043 participants (25.7%); 46 of 50 cohorts used DSM-III-R or DSM-IV criteria.

reporting_issues.note: Figure 2 adds a third version, random effects 0.46 (0.37 to 0.55).
The Results 4th paragraph values are those of Figure 2's random-effects totals.
Figure 2 also prints 92% and 74%, but its inpatient Q statistic (11.41 on 6 df, P < .08) implies I2 of about 47% and non-significant heterogeneity, although the text calls it significant; see missed.
P for chi-square 0.172 recomputed: 0.68 (1 df), 0.92 (2 df). The abstract prints only P < .001, not the chi-square values.
The Discussion 1st paragraph also says no association with sex, so the Conclusions contradict the Discussion as well.
Recomputed: 48 cohort mean ages, mean 29.94, SD 9.00 (median of cohort means 30.85).
Table 1's cohort size x CUD% sums to exactly 8,275 over 20,619 participants, so the count comes from Table 1 and its matching proportion is 40.1%.
My count of Table 1: United States 37, Australia 4, Germany 3, France 2, Brazil, Canada, Netherlands, New Zealand 1 each; DSM-IV 38, DSM-III-R 8, DSM-5 4.
In addition, the Results 2nd paragraph lists references 19, 21, 22, 23, 24 and 31 under the SCID, while Table 1 gives operationalized criteria or a diary for them.
The Methods sentence is ambiguous (its 'criteria' may mean the diagnostic criteria that Table 1 does give), but no cohort's definition of regular use appears in Table 1 either way.
Titles of references 32 and 35 both name NESARC.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low confidence agreed: on my reading items 2, 4, 7, 11 and 13 are not met (reference 13 is the PROSPERO home page accessed after the search, with no registration number; English only; no list of excluded studies in the article or among the supplement's listed contents; one headline estimate pooled across settings and timeframes at I2 99.2%; quality not used in interpreting results). Item 16 'no' also agreed (checked 2026-10-31): the notes declare the two authors' interests, and the author contributions say Seitz obtained funding, but no funding statement names its source.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. All five gaps verified (Key Points and Discussion 1st paragraph present 47% as the share who will experience withdrawal; Conclusions on men; Abstract › Importance calls withdrawal a diagnostic indicator of use disorder; Discussion 2nd paragraph on symptoms mistaken for anxiety or depression).

missed: Figure 2 (forest plot, an image) gives estimates the card does not record: random effects overall 0.46 (0.37 to 0.55); fixed effect overall 0.28 (0.27 to 0.28) and by setting 0.19, 0.52 and 0.82; event counts summing to 6,469 (3,245; 2,929; 295). The abstract's count is therefore the forest plot's event total, and the review itself prints the participant-level 28%.

Figure 2 prints the inpatient heterogeneity as chi-square 11.41 on 6 df, P < .08, I2 74%: that Q gives I2 of about 47% and P = .077 (editors' calculation), so heterogeneity among the 7 inpatient cohorts is not significant, though the Results 5th paragraph calls it significant (I2 74%) and Table 2 gives 94%, P < .001. The other Q values match their I2 (population 98%, outpatient 92%, overall 99%).
The Results 2nd paragraph assigns the SCID to the cohorts that Table 1 lists with operationalized criteria or a self-reported diary (references 19, 21, 22, 23, 24, 31).
The Discussion 1st paragraph states that withdrawal was not associated with sex, contradicting the Conclusions as well as Table 2.
Minor: sample.selection_effects gives clinical participants as 6,041 (text's 357 inpatients); Table 1 and Figure 2 give 6,043 (25.7%).

Funding field confirmed against the article notes: no funding statement; 'Obtained funding: Seitz' under author contributions; Bahji, a Canadian Institutes of Health Research Master's scholarship; Seitz, site investigator for a Hoffmann La Roche-sponsored trial; a librarian helped develop the search (Additional Contributions).
